newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO commander demands Karadzic turn himself in.
newsitem.headline: NATO commander demands Karadzic turn himself in.

text.p: NATO's supreme commander, U.S. General Wesley Clark, hinted on Thursday that time may be running out for fugitive former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic, an indicted war criminal.
"I am encouraging Mr Karadzic to turn himself soon.
"I'm not setting a time limit, I'm saying turn yourself in soon. I am not going to speculate on the 'if not'," Clark told reporters.
The Western alliance commander delivered the warning in the mountain village of Pale outside Sarajevo, which serves as headquarters for Karadzic.
The wartime Bosnian Serb president has been indicted twice by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague but continues to wield power covertly in Bosnia's Serb-controlled territory.
Karadzic, an ultra-nationalist who opposed the 1995 Dayton peace treaty on Bosnia, stepped down under U.S.-led pressure a year ago but has broken a pledge to stay out of Bosnia's post-war politics.
Since NATO pounced on two Karadzic allies last month who were also wanted for war crimes, speculation has been building that the former Serb leader might be arrested or even spirited out of Bosnia.

Speaking only three km (two miles) from Karadzic's home, Clark indicated that the NATO-led peace force would no longer tolerate unauthorised special police units that guard war crimes indictees such as Karadzic.

"With respect to whoever may be guarding Radovan Karadzic, I don't know right now but obviously the police as they are restructured are going to be performing only those tasks which are legal," he said.

Clark ordered the multinational Stabilisation Force (SFOR) last week to treat special police in Bosnia as military forces in a crackdown clearly aimed at dismantling the backbone of Karadzic's authority.
Under the country's peace treaty, NATO could have supervised special police units previously.
Clark said NATO decided to move against special police this month to speed up implementation of the slow-moving peace process in former Yugoslavia.
"The reason it's being implemented now is it is clear we need to move forward more rapidly to attain the objectives of the Dayton (peace) agreement," he said.
At one point a middle-aged man who identified himself as a former Bosnian Serb soldier told Clark to "please leave Radovan Karadzic alone".
Clark told the man that his own leaders had pledged under the peace treaty to hand over indicted war criminals such as Karadzic and his former army commander, General Ratko Mladic.
"I would appeal to those men who have been indicted to have the courage to turn themselves in voluntarily and face the charges against them in a court of international law," he said.
NATO officers said earlier that peacekeeping troops were on heightened alert as a result of an unspecified security threat to an SFOR base in the Sarajevo area in Moslem-Croat federation territory.
After the NATO raid on two suspected war criminals last month in Serb territory, international monitors and NATO soldiers were targeted in a wave of retaliatory bombings.
But Clark said the alliance-led peace force would not be intimidated by possible revenge attacks.
"No one should misunderstand that although we seek peace and came in peace, we can protect ourselves."
